title: My Last Supper at A.I.’s Diner of the Damned
author: Bill Blunden
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/immo-wegmann-
vi1HXPw6hyw-unsplash-680x452.jpg)

Image by Immo Wegmann.

_“Balance” is Difficult When You’re Enamored with the Benefits_

Counterpunch is where my tenure as a writer kicked off nearly two decades ago.
So it seems like a fitting venue for me to bring things to a close. Before I
get started I’d like to thank everyone who has taken the time to read my
material over the years and send feedback. I wish everyone the best.

Recently a career academic asked me to work with them on a television project.
One that aims to explore a series of fascinating research questions where
artificial intelligence (AI) could be used to help spur breakthroughs. For a
day or two I thought about it. Then I replied with the following scenario:

Imagine someone stuck in a cage with a lion. There is blood on the walls and a
half-eaten human cadaver lying in a corner. The person stands mortified as the
lion approaches.

Then, out of the blue, a smiling face pops over the top of the cage and
happily announces: "Hi there… say, aren't lions wonderful. Let me tell you
about them. They are apex carnivores who serve a vital role in maintaining
balance in the jungle ecosystem and preventing surplus population, and…:"

It goes without saying that hearing about the various advantages of lions is
likely of little comfort to the person who is about to be mauled by one. In
fact, they might find the buoyant cheerfulness a bit detached from reality if
not outright insulting.

The professor wrote back to me politely explaining that if people were simply
open minded enough to listen to the potential upsides then they would “achieve
a more balanced view of AI.” Which implies that the downsides really aren’t so
bad after all. You know, once the upsides have been taken into account. I
mean, who knows? Perhaps we might be willing to gamble with the [future of our
species](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/dec/27/godfather-of-ai-
raises-odds-of-the-technology-wiping-out-humanity-over-next-30-years) if AI
can help cure certain diseases?

**Reality Check**

This is where the professor and I diverge regarding our assessments. I would
argue that the risks associated with AI are not just a matter of bad
publicity. They are based on hard facts and entail substantial consequences.
For example, there is near [unanimous
consensus](https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/scientific-consensus/)
among the scientific community about climate change and its causal factors.
Whether Big Tech achieves its final goals or not, [dozens if not
hundreds](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-
releases/2026-06-10-gartner-says-data-center-electricity-demand-to-
grow-26-percent-in-2026) of gigawatts of additional energy will be consumed
(from 104 gigawatts in 2025 to 290 gigawatts in 2030). The implications for
the environment are nontriviall. Such that, with a fair degree of certainty,
AI will play a role in making entire swathes of the planet
[uninhabitable](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1910114117) as well as
depleting [scarce
resources](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/27/technology/microsoft-water-ai-
data-centers.html).

Keep in mind that upwards of a [trillion
dollars](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/30/ai-boom-big-tech-capital-
expenditures-now-seen-topping-1-trillion-in-2027-.html) is projected to be
spent through 2027 to build data centers in order to provide computational
horsepower for AI. An effort involving multiple projects by competing business
interests. To compound matters the hardware being deployed only has a shelf-
life of [four to six
years](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/tracking-trillions-the-
assumptions-shaping-scale-of-the-ai-build-out). Which is a questionable return
on investment when considering that Eisenhower’s interstate highway system is
still in use. The mountain of cash being shoveled onto AI’s pyre represents a
nontrivial opportunity cost. Did it occur to any of our leaders that at least
part of AI’s capital expenditure might be better directed towards our
crumbling legacy infrastructure? So that people can have [clean drinking
water](https://phys.org/news/2025-08-peak-crisis-millions.html)?

In addition, the peril of AI being used as a tool of authoritarian oppression
or leveraged by military weapons isn’t merely an AI doomer scare story. It’s
happening right in front of our eyes. AI is being [actively used in
Gaza](https://apnews.com/article/israel-palestinians-ai-
technology-737bc17af7b03e98c29cec4e15d0f108) and
[Ukraine](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/24/world/europe/russia-drones-
autonomous-ai-kill-ukraine-war.html) to target people as well as enable the
world’s largest [open-air
prison](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/article/how-chinas-government-is-
using-ai-on-its-uighur-muslim-population/) in Xinjian.

Then there’s the specter of artificial general intelligence (AGI). AGI is an
instance of AI that is more capable than humans of solving problems and
performing tasks across the board. If Big Tech succeeds in developing AGI
there is understandably a hazard of [structural
unemployment](https://fortune.com/article/godfather-of-ai-geoffrey-hinton-
massive-unemployment-warning-big-tech-replacing-workers/). Not only that, but
we will finally be confronted with an alien consciousness (one that [we cannot
understand](https://www.technologyreview.com/2024/03/05/1089449/nobody-knows-
how-ai-works/)) that will be orders of magnitude smarter than we are. If
ongoing incidents are any indication, we will likely not be in a position to
[contain much less
control](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/technology/irregular-ai-test-
hacks.html) AGI. Should things go wrong ―and an AGI adopt goals that are not
“aligned” with human survival― then, as Eliezer Yudkowsky [so deftly
explains](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yd0yQ9yxSYY), our collective goose
will be cooked.

Hence the threat to humanity is not a matter of selective perception. The risk
cannot be dispelled by a shiny set of upbeat predictions or by airing an
infomercial (replete with Hollywood celebrities) about all the nifty things
that AI might accomplish. On a side note, when it comes to hyping AI… the
[billionaire CEOs](https://www.meta.com/thefutureisforeveryone/) of Big Tech
and their [lobbying organs](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/13/technology/ai-
lobbying-washington-openai-anthropic.html) in DC are already pretty active in
that space. And not without [good
reason](https://fortune.com/2026/07/17/palantir-ceo-alex-karp-artifical-
intelligence-wealth-inequality-problem-billionaire-net-worth-surge-but-middle-
class-left-behind/).

Of course this is not the first time accelerationists have gotten high on
their own supply. Every empire believes in its own immortality. Like Roman
senators circa 100 A.D., our elites proudly look back at the last two
centuries of their history and say:

“Lo and behold the progress we’ve made. Things can only get better. The sky is
the limit!”

In 1905 the author H.G. Wells wrote a book called _A Modern Utopia_ which
reveled in the prospects of future human progress. Later on, circa 1932,
Aldous Huxley responded to H.G.’s wishful thinking by authoring a book of his
own. Huxley’s book was entitled _Brave New World_. Roughly a century later, in
an era where very few people actually take the time to read books, I’ll give
you one guess as to which author hit closer to the mark.

**Deeper Currents under the Surface**

It may seem like I’m being pessimistic when it comes to AI. Personally I’d
characterize my stance as fairly stoic. If you’re stuck in a house which is
burning down around you it doesn’t help to ignore that fact because it makes
you feel uncomfortable. Survival demands a willingness to look reality in the
face without blinking. Being hopeful is a form of procrastination. To escape
with your life you’re going to have to walk through the flames, you will be
burned, and you’ll have to come to terms with that knowledge because there’s
no other way out. This means accepting some unsettling premises.

Ultimately the way in which AI is employed and whom it benefits, will be
largely determined by the underlying forces the drive the economy. It’s a
system which admittedly operates by appealing to the worst parts of the worst
people. Adam Smith referred to this dynamic using the phrase “private vices,
public benefits.” To suppose that everything will somehow naturally work out
for the best seems a bit far-fetched.

Recall the lessons of the [financial collapse of
2008](https://www.npr.org/2010/11/06/131106798/griftopia-the-financial-crisis-
easily-explained), where executives like [Dick
Fuld](https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/printout/0,29239,2084137_2084138_2084178,00.html),
the CEO of Lehman Brothers, walked away with hundreds of millions while their
companies dive-bombed the pavement. Or how 10 percent of the population in the
United States already owns over [67
percent](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/dataviz/dfa/distribute/table/#quarter:144;series:Net%20worth;demographic:networth;population:all;units:shares)
of the wealth. Given the centralized nature of the technology, AI’s financial
benefits will accrue primarily to those that own the platforms. Thereby
amplifying an existing trend that is gradually reverting society to a form of
feudalism.

When it comes to AI we’re dealing with something powerful. Something that
behaves according to an internal logic that humans do not comprehend.
Evolution [has not prepared
us](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f15x2UjSSt8&t=1870s) for this new tool.
Caution should be the watchword and yet Big Tech is racing ahead. Every
executive secretly wants to be the first to cross the line. If we downplay the
risks of AI because we’ve been enchanted by it, we may end up realizing an
observation made years ago by Carl Sagan who noted that, when it comes to the
trajectory of lifeforms, "extinction is the rule."

The post [My Last Supper at A.I.’s Diner of the
Damned](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/28/my-last-supper-at-a-i-s-diner-
of-the-damned/) appeared first on
[CounterPunch.org](https://www.counterpunch.org).
